item.title: Can Visiting Sex Clubs Be Good for Gay Men?
item.description:
Sex

Can Visiting Sex Clubs Be Good for Gay Men?

It may be surprising, but visiting sex clubs can enhance gay men's well-being.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Sex clubs help gay men embrace sexual diversity, healing, and authentic self-expression.
  • Sex clubs offer gay men a judgment-free space that counters minority stress and discrimination.
  • For some gay men, sex clubs nurture queer spirituality and expansive definitions of love.
Source: VladOrlov / iStock

Talking about visiting sex clubs is frowned upon in society. Some gay men enjoy visiting gay sex clubs on a regular basis, and that regularity is often seen as negative by society and loaded with moral judgments. As a psychotherapist working with many gay men, I have noticed that many of them report increased well-being as a result of visiting sexualised spaces. Within the societal noise of moral judgment, it is difficult to hear nuance in those conversations, but it is important not to shame gay men whose lives do not fit in with societal expectations.

What are gay sex clubs?

Gay sex clubs are adult-only, men-only sexualised spaces. An increasing number of “men-only” establishments include "all men," which means that trans men are welcome. too.

Most gay sex clubs offer different options for sexual and erotic connections; for example, booths for one-to-one (or three) people wanting to have sex in private, and more open spaces for people who enjoy group sex and/or enjoy “public” sex (i.e., being watched or watching). Some gay sex clubs have special nights such as “Naked Only” nights (also called “Boots Only”), and some sex clubs specialise in kink, catering to the diverse kinky community with stricter dress codes (leather, Lycra, and sports gear, for example). Some sexualised places can be “wet” ones, also called gay saunas, offering a pool, sauna, and steam rooms; the dress code is usually naked with a towel around the waist. Gay sex clubs also provide condoms and lube for free. Most establishments have a no-drug policy (other than poppers).

How can visiting gay sex clubs be good for gay men?

In my therapeutic work with gay men, I have observed several benefits for gay, bisexual, queer men and men who have sex with men visiting gay sex clubs that enhance their well-being:

  • Countering minority stress
  • Having an antidote to shame and societal discrimination
  • Embracing sex-positivity, body-positivity, and age-positivity
  • Having a sense of meaningful belonging
  • Connecting to expansive love and queer spirituality

It may sound surprising, as it is not the narrative we often hear on this topic because not many people talk about it openly for fear of being judged or shamed. In my privilege of being a psychotherapist and providing a private, confidential, and sex-positive space where gay men can feel comfortable talking honestly about their own sexual, erotic, intimate, and social experiences, I have heard many stories of enhanced well-being as a result of visiting sex clubs. Let’s look at the benefits in more detail.

article continues after advertisement

Countering minority stress. Minority stress is the chronic, cumulative stress experienced by marginalised people in society. Gay men (and other minorities) experience minority stress on a regular basis, experiencing prejudice and discrimination just for being who they are.

In my consulting room, many gay men tell me that visiting gay sex clubs is a significant buffer against minority stress because those sexualised spaces tend to be non-judgmental and up for intimate connections, whereas it is for a chat or physical contact. It is a space where gay men feel they can just be themselves, without editing themselves to make others comfortable, and without any fear of discrimination. They can also engage with others as much or as little as they wish. Many gay men report those spaces as being safe spaces away from the rest of the difficult world out there.

Having an antidote to shame and societal discrimination. Gay men’s sex clubs can provide a safe space for a meaningful connection with one’s sexuality, affirming their sexual desires and turn-ons without shame. Some gay men experience it as a form of existential freedom, where they connect in the here-and-now with their mind-body connection in feeling alive and connecting with other sex-positive gay men in that space, enhancing a sense of legitimacy and belonging. It can be an essential component to counter social discrimination such as homophobia, heteronormativity, and mononormativity.

Embracing sex-positivity, body-positivity, and age-positivity. The mainstream gay men’s scene can be harsh too, because it promotes a high standard of beauty and status; it can be body-shaming and ageist. Many gay men struggle with their body image or with aging because of those high standards.

Visiting gay sex clubs can help soothe those struggles because most people tend to be accepting of each other, and it can be a welcoming, safe place for all gay men to feel “good enough” regardless of their body shape, age, penis size, status, or kink. Of course, it doesn’t mean that all gay men in the sex club would want to have sex with each other. There is a strong emphasis on consent in gay sex clubs that is expressed not only through words but also through eye contact, facial expression, and body language. In a gay sex club, saying “no” to someone’s touch is usually done with respect and without shame.

Having a sense of meaningful belonging. As mentioned above, gay men don’t go to sex clubs only for sex; for some, it can be a place of social connection in an environment that is non-judgmental, unlike the mainstream gay scene and the heteronormative society. The social connections in those sexualised spaces can be affirming of queer sexualities, where people can be free to just be themselves. For example, it could be just having a drink at the bar naked, chatting to another naked man. For many gay men, these are the only spaces where they don’t feel societal oppression. Gay sex clubs are often described as honest spaces that are unapologetically queer with sexual and erotic freedom. They can be valuable spaces to relax and make honest and meaningful connections, even if it is just for one night. This fosters a genuine sense of belonging that is essential for well-being.

article continues after advertisement

Connecting to expansive love and queer spirituality. For some gay men, visiting gay sex clubs is associated with an expansive definition of love and "queer spirituality." In the heteronormative and mononormative constructs, we are taught that love exists within a romantic relationship. But in queer spaces, love goes beyond that. Love can mean loving multiple people at once. Love can occur through a brief sexual encounter in a sex club as part of loving themselves, their communities, and sexualities. For some gay men, expansive love is being in touch with their queer spirituality. Being naked and/or in sexual spaces with each other can feel highly spiritual, plugging in to their queer energy, affirming their sexuality and their existence as part of nature. It can be a great source of healing and well-being.

Gay sex clubs can be the perfect spaces to create and maintain queer joy, queer spirituality, expansive love, and genuine belonging. Gay sex clubs are not the sordid, sleazy, dark places for sad old gay men that some people assume them to be. They can be spaces where sex is celebrated, not shamed, and a place that can feel sacred in its honesty of sexual and erotic diversity and community celebrations.

item.title: Getting in Shape With Silence
item.description:
Anxiety

Getting in Shape With Silence

Most of us are not bad at silence, we are just out of shape with it.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Silence often feels threatening because it exposes avoided thoughts and emotions.
  • Building tolerance for silence is like muscle training—start small and increase gradually.
  • High-achievers may mistake constant input for productivity, when it's often avoidance.
Source: Maxim Boldyrev/Pexels

A client of mine, a high-achiever I will call Dana, came into a session and announced a victory that would sound small to most people. She had driven in complete silence. There was no podcast, no playlist, no phone call, no audiobook playing. It was just her, the road, and her own thoughts for the length of a short drive to her therapy session. This was something that terrified her. In fact, just being solely in her own company had frightened her for as long as she could remember. So naturally, we made this a treatment goal.

When she first described the fear, it was vivid. She imagined that the moment she turned everything off, the thoughts she had spent years pushing down would come rushing back and crash into her like a tidal wave. So she kept the noise on. Every commute, every errand, and every quiet moment got filled. The stimulation felt like a preference, but it was actually a strategy.

This is the part most people miss. The constant input was not background noise. She was conditioning herself, and the distraction was doing a job. The podcasts and playlists were keeping difficult material at a distance, which meant that silence was never neutral for her. Silence could ignite discomfort and bring unwanted thoughts or emotions up to the surface. Lots of effort had gone into keeping this very pattern at bay, simply because turning off the noise meant facing whatever the noise had been holding back.

Source: Keenan-Constance/Pexels

Her treatment goal was built the way you build anything you are afraid of, in small and deliberate doses, very similar to immersion therapy tactics. She did not start with a long silent drive. She started with a few minutes and worked up from there. This helped her get in shape with the silence, gain comfort, and build self-trust. After several attempts, she came in and said the sentence that matters most in this kind of work. "I did it. It wasn't as bad as I thought it would be."

That gap is where the change happens. Anxiety is future-based thinking, usually overpreparing. Our internal bodyguards have the steering wheel, and they consistently overpredict how bad something will feel and how long the feeling will last. Dana had organized years of behavior around a catastrophe that, when she finally tested it, never actually arrived. The silence was uncomfortable. It was not the tidal wave. Her brain had been bracing against a threat far smaller than advertised, and the only way to learn that was to find out.

The soreness is the point

I told her that what she was doing was a form of getting in shape. When you start training a muscle that has been idle, you get sore. The soreness is not an injury. It is the tissue adapting. The mistake an anxious mind makes is reading that early discomfort as danger and stopping. With silence, the discomfort is the rep working. Stay with it in tolerable doses and the soreness starts to fade, the same way it does in the gym. You are not eliminating the discomfort by avoiding it. You are building the capacity to hold it.

A few things follow from that comparison. You do not begin with the heaviest weight, which is why the small doses were the actual work and not a watered-down version of it. You cannot just hope a muscle gets stronger, and you cannot force your way into tolerating silence through sheer effort either. Capacity is built through repetition. And "being out of shape" with sitting with yourself is not a character flaw. Most of us live in a constantly stimulated environment and are simply deconditioned.

Why this hits high performers hardest

For the high-performers and chronic fixers I work with, this runs deeper than a noisy commute. The inability to sit unstimulated often disguises itself as drive. Constant input feels like productivity, but much of the time it is avoidance. The same person who cannot drive in silence frequently cannot rest, cannot be unproductive, and reaches to solve other people's problems partly so they never have to sit with their own. Silence threatens that entire arrangement, which is exactly why it feels so threatening. The quiet drive is a small rep for a much larger capacity, the ability to be with something difficult without immediately reaching to fix it, fill it, or numb it.

I want to be clear that this is not meditation. There is no app, no breath count, no posture, and no goal of emptying your mind. You are not performing a technique. You are removing the buffer and staying present to whatever shows up. That is a lower bar than formal practice, and for a lot of people it transfers more directly into daily life. You are clearing your internal clutter deliberately and preventing a massive pop that usually takes longer to recover from.

Source: Khush Sanhu/Pexels

What surfaces in the quiet is not always profound, either. Sometimes it is grief, or a decision you have been avoiding. Sometimes it is a grocery list. The practice is staying, not demanding or creating pressure to be productive.

One caution, then a place to start

Dana did this inside therapy, with support and in graded steps. For someone with a trauma history, severe untreated anxiety, or intrusive thoughts, dropping all stimulation at once can flood the system rather than build tolerance. If silence reliably overwhelms you, that is information worth bringing to a professional rather than pushing through alone.

If you want to try it, start absurdly small. Drive to the end of the street with the radio off, or stay quiet for the length of one song. Then turn it back on. You have full permission to. This works just as well with walks. The reps are what build the capacity at your pace. Over time, the silence stops feeling like a threat and starts feeling like a place you can actually be. And the truth is, as long as you are breathing, you will always be with you.

item.title: You Can Talk to Your Child About Anything
item.description:
Parenting

You Can Talk to Your Child About Anything

Parents avoid difficult conversations with children, but they don't have to.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • You can talk to your child about anything.
  • You have to be honest and direct.
  • Allow your child to ask as many questions as they want.

Frequently, people come to me asking how to talk with their children about topics such as sex, porn, and yes, death. They feel they don't know where to start and feel guilty for avoiding these topics. They are nervous about saying the wrong thing and worry that they will unintentionally traumatize their children.

But it isn't so hard! Here are a few basic principles to guide you.

First, always be honest. In almost every situation, it is better to tell your child the truth rather than make something up that you think will be easier for them to take.

Second, be direct. Don't beat around the bush or make unhelpful analogies.

Third, tell your child only as much as you think they can handle given their age and stage of development, while still being honest.

Fourth, let your child ask questions and answer them as best you can. Doing this lets you know what is on your child's mind about the topic. Their questions will guide you and show you where to go with the discussion. Allowing them to ask as many questions as they need to also gives your child the message that they can come back to you and ask more.

Breaking it down by age and stage of development:

Toddlers and Pre-schoolers: Be concrete. Name feelings, Reassure them, if you can, that it is alright to think about this subject and that you will be there to answer any questions they have.

School Age Kids: Add more nuance to your explanations. At this age, children are more emotionally mature and can understand more complex issues. They will probably already have thought about whatever issue you want to talk with them about, and they will have their own feelings and opinions.

Teens: Talk to teens almost as if you are talking to a peer. At this age, kids are very sensitive to being talked down to. Ask their opinions and have a discussion (if they will let you) about the topic at hand.

Talking about tough topics strengthens your child’s ability to think, solve problems, communicate, and build resilience. Doing so early and often also gives you a chance to prevent your child from hearing about these things first from peers and other unreliable sources, and it also gives you a chance to explain these things from the vantage point of your own values and beliefs.

item.title: A Dream Deferred
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

A Dream Deferred

Personal Perspective: What happens when you stop waiting for the right time?

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • The life you want does not appear when conditions are perfect; it appears when you decide to make it happen.
  • High achievers who lead sustainable careers are those who practice rest and self-care regularly.
  • Modeling joy and intentional living for others is an act of leadership and courage in choosing oneself first.

For years, I had a dream I kept putting off.

This dream was born from an exercise about what my ideal day would look like. In my vision, I woke up every morning without an alarm, with nowhere to be, and nothing in particular I had to accomplish except to enjoy my life. I felt fulfilled, happy, and present, challenging myself and learning, creating lasting memories with my family.

In my dream, I immersed myself in foreign lands, soaking up culture, tasting extraordinary foods, and experiencing life at a slow pace. I was surrounded by nature and felt deeply connected to myself again.

This was a dream I kept putting off every year. Because the fear always shows up right on schedule.

An extended trip? Can you really be away that long? What about your work and patients?

Do you know how much this is going to cost?

Two sets of traditional ethnic parents. Are you out of your mind? How are they going to get along? What if they hate every second of it? What if everyone's miserable and you spent all this money and came home with nothing but regret?

Your brain will make every excuse. Because it's scared. Because dreaming big means you might actually have to do the thing, and doing the thing means it could fail, or that the gap between the dream and reality is wider than you had imagined.

I also know what it looks like to defer your life. Becoming a physician is the ultimate delayed gratification. I’ve lived it. I'm a physician, a mom, and a coach. I know what it’s like to put my patients, residents, and colleagues, and the needs of my daughter and family before my own. The same goes for the doctors I work with. They are some of the most brilliant, dedicated people I have ever met. They, like how I used to be, sometimes forget that they are more than their occupation and work.

I write about this. I speak about it. I coach many clients on it. And yet I wasn’t taking my own advice.

There's a difference between moving from burnout to a sustainable career, and moving from living your life to actually loving it. I've done the first. The second requires something more intentional.

As a physician and as someone who has done her own hard inner work, I know that we are exceptional at giving advice we never take ourselves. We tell the people we love that preventative care matters. That you shouldn’t wait for something drastic to happen before you realize you have to start taking care of yourself.

I know that the life you want does not materialize on its own. It doesn't magically appear once the work is done or the schedule opens up or the kids get older or things finally feel stable. It appears when you decide with intention, with commitment, with the willingness to disappoint a few people along the way.

So I decided.

And I wanted my daughter to watch me decide. To grow up knowing that her mother chose joy out loud and without apology. That the woman who works so hard also rests deeply. That loving your work and loving your family and loving yourself are not competing priorities, they are the whole point of this one precious life.

I watched my own mother pour herself out for everyone around her, always saving herself for last… if there was anything left at all. I understand that because I have lived it. And I wasn’t happy carrying that burden, and living under conditions someone else made up for me. I refuse to pass that particular inheritance to my daughter.

So when the nudge got loud enough, saying, You've been wanting to do this forever, so why haven't you?—I finally listened.

3 generations, 2 ethnicities, 1 big happy family somewhere in Southern France
Source: Cynthia Chen-Joea

I booked three weeks in southern France with my husband, my daughter, my mom, and my in-laws, with a huge family van and no agenda beyond being present and experiencing life together.

And here's the thing: Once you achieve one dream, the high is real. The gratification is real. And suddenly, you are on a roll and believe that you can do anything. You start to believe that the next dream is possible, too. And then the one after that.

That momentum is what I've been riding, and it's what finally got me here, experiencing yet another dream of mine this year.

Showing up for myself is part of showing up for everyone else, and contrary to what many believe when they start doing things for themselves, that's not selfish.

The people who build sustainable and fulfilling lives in medicine, in parenting, in any demanding career, are not the ones who sacrificed everything. They're the ones who learned that rest and self-care are not a reward you earn at the end, but practices you start from the very beginning.

Three weeks in southern France is not just a vacation.

It's a declaration.

It's me prioritizing my values, putting them in my calendar, and protecting them fiercely. And sure, there have been heated moments and a couple of tears, but there have also been afternoons spent playing outside in the sun and grass, poolside adventures across three generations, and chirping birds waking me up every morning. With no alarm and nowhere to be, and nothing in particular to accomplish except to be present with the people I love the most.

And isn’t that the dream? A life of downs and the most extraordinary ups, memories that last a lifetime, and presence in this one and only precious thing we call life.

item.title: 7 Ways to Make Yourself Happy While Saving the Planet
item.description:
Environment

7 Ways to Make Yourself Happy While Saving the Planet

Positive psychology versus doomsday thinking on climate change.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Most people have strong negative feelings about climate change and environmental destruction.
  • But anger, frustration, guilt, and anxiety can lead us to feel hopeless rather than triggering action.
  • A new book suggests the key to saving the world might be making small choices that make us happy.

The majority of North Americans have strong feelings about climate change, but those feelings are mostly unpleasant—anxiety, sadness, anger, confusion, frustration, and guilt. Well-intentioned attempts to spur action often amplify those negative feelings with alarming statistics about how much worse things are getting. This can lead to a sense of helplessness, and research findings suggest such approaches can actually make things worse (see Cialdini et al., 2006).

Is there a happier path to a healthier planet?

Maybe there is a better way to go. In an engaging new book integrating insights from positive psychology and the science of sustainability, UBC psychologists Liz Dunn and Jiaying Zhao suggest we focus on green choices that make ourselves feel happier (rather than guiltier or angrier).

Liz Dunn is a positive psychologist, who found that spending money on other people makes us happier than spending on ourselves (see "Are you spending money in ways that make you unhappy?"). Jiaying Zhao is an expert on the psychology of sustainability. Their book Leave the lights on: How joyful decisions can save our species is full of research-based hints about how to make yourself feel good while acting to save the planet. It's also full of facts about the shockingly high carbon impact of some everyday choices, such as buying new jeans, or choosing beef over tofu for lunch (you can also check out Wynes and Nicholas 2017, and this website from University of Michigan).

Dunn and Zhao's new book.
Source: Dunn and Zhao, used with permission

Here are a few suggestions for saving the planet and making yourself happier at the same time:

1. Get out of the traffic jam

Commuting is not only unpleasant, but it raises your blood pressure. When I asked the authors, they put biking instead of driving at the top of their green happiness list. My son Dave and I both gave up our parking passes, making it easier to take a nice bike ride instead of driving in traffic to pay $15 for a hard-to-find parking space. Going completely car-free is an option in some places; and given the costs of car payments, insurance, gasoline, auto repairs, and parking, it could be cheaper for many of us to take an Uber, use local mass transit, and rent an electric vehicle for any long car trips.

2. Save money and hassles with a stay-cation

Getting on a jet plane has an exceptionally big carbon footprint, and it's also often unpleasant. Yet most people haven't visited the tourist attractions and great restaurants in their own areas. Renting a room at a local hotel, or setting a local vacation agenda from home, saves the hassle of air travel—missed flights, cramped seats, overpriced airport food and drinks, lost luggage, jetlag, and thousands of dollars in flight costs. If you must fly, the authors note that taking direct flights and using only carry-on luggage can reduce your carbon footprint.

3. Trade some threads with the neighbors

I was amazed to discover that the fashion industry generates twice the global emissions of all airline flights and shipping combined. Jeans may be a particularly environmentally toxic purchase, generating massive amounts of carbon and wasting immense amounts of water. Their suggestions including buying fewer new clothes, or joining a group that gives clothing to one another. Most of us have lots of clothes we hardly ever wear that someone else might enjoy, and they might have something we’d like, especially if it were free.

4. Get your retirement funds out of hidden fossil fuel investments

I was surprised to learn that about 20% of money invested with a major bank is invested in the fossil fuel industry (even though those are not particularly good investments these days). Author Jiaying Zhao suggests looking for the best green banks in your area at https://bank.green/sustainable-eco-banks/.

5. Eat more fruits and vegetables

If you choose a spicy tofu and veggie dish instead of cheesesteak, or a blueberry and almond butter smoothie over a chocolate ice cream bar, you’ll not only make yourself healthier and leaner, but you’ll also reduce your carbon footprint. The authors describe one restaurant that used to list their meat option first, then their fish option, with vegetarian options "available on request." Hardly anybody chose the veggie option, and the meat dish was most popular, but when they put the veggie option first, there was a dramatic reversal in what customers ordered. At home, they suggest taking fruits and veggies out of those hidden bins at the bottom of the fridge, and putting them front and center so they turn into meals rather than science projects. You don’t have to go full vegetarian to make a big impact, but as the authors suggest, you can “make meat a treat.”

6. Act locally

It’s easy to feel overwhelmed thinking about petrochemical industry lobbyists blocking the path of global progress in Washington, D.C. But many important decisions are made locally. Regional public commissions can close coal plants, for instance, and city councilors can vote in better bike lanes. So, a little time spent contacting local politicians can have an outsized impact.

7. Make saving the world a social event

It feels good to hang out with other people, and neighbors really influence one another (about whether to buy solar panels or electric cars, for instance). Many of their suggestions involve teaming up with friends and neighbors—carpooling, clothes trading, and healthy group lunches, for example. Combining this suggestion with the last one, another of the authors’ favorite suggestions is to host a voting party before local elections (where voting is less likely but each vote counts a lot more).

Besides being full of great ideas, I found the book a sheer pleasure to read. After self-indulgently reading mysteries for the last week, I expected it might be onerous to get through an academic book, especially on a topic that oftens makes me feel guilty, angry, and anxious. But I was pleasantly surprised to discover that it was harder to put down Dunn and Zhao’s book than those mysteries I’d been reading. And reading Leave the Lights On made me feel a lot more hopeful and happy. Given that I live in the “Valley of the Sun,” I’m now looking into getting solar panels for my house. Following the last recommendation above, I’ll be sure to put them on the street-facing side, so my neighbors can see them.
